_comment: THE SECURITY HEADERS, AND THE ONE PLACE THEY ARE WRITTEN DOWN.
This file is the source of truth. The nginx snippet on the server is
rendered from it (scripts/check_security_headers.py --render), and the
gate checks the live site against it, so the server's copy cannot drift
away from this one without the gate going red.
'mode' says which header name the server is sending:
report-only - the browser reports what it would have blocked
enforce    - the browser blocks it
Both are checked against the same policy below, so flipping the mode
means changing this file AND the nginx snippet together - and the
gate notices if only one of them moved.
The allow lists are measured, not guessed: the origins the browser
really asked for, and the browser features the code really uses.
'unsafe-inline' in script-src is not a shortcut - Next.js's static
export writes its flight data into 250 different inline scripts, one
set per page, so their hashes cannot be listed in a header and would
change with every edit.

whyInherit: In nginx a location that declares ANY add_header does not inherit
the ones from the server block - it replaces them. The
.html page was served with no HSTS, no nosniff, no X-Frame-Options
and no Referrer-Policy. `add_header_inherit merge;` makes a
location keep its own header AND inherit the server's.

_comment: One address per kind of nginx location, because the headers have to
be on all of them. The .html addresses and /assets/ are the ones
that used to lose them.
